title: Why is Incredible Hulk #181 so valuable?
answer: Incredible Hulk #181 (November 1974) is the first full appearance of Wolverine, the most popular character Marvel created after the 1960s, and it is the most valuable comic of the Bronze Age. Demand comes from Wolverine's decades as an X-Men and film lead; supply in high grade is limited by ordinary 1974 print runs, by the Marvel Value Stamp many readers cut from the issue, and by fifty years of handling.
body:
## What is in the issue

Len Wein's story, drawn by Herb Trimpe, is a three-way fight in the Canadian wilderness between the Hulk, the Wendigo and the newly introduced Wolverine, sent by the Canadian government as "Weapon X". Wolverine had been glimpsed in the last panel of #180; #181 is the first issue in which he does anything. John Romita Sr. designed the yellow-and-blue costume.

## Why the demand is so deep

Wolverine joined the new X-Men in 1975 and became the franchise's lead through the Claremont years, the 1990s boom and every X-Men film since 2000. The book is wanted by X-Men collectors, Hulk collectors, Bronze Age key collectors and investors at once. No other 1970s book has that breadth.

## Why supply in high grade is thin

1. **The Marvel Value Stamp.** The issue contains stamp #54 (Shanna the She-Devil) on an interior page. Many copies had it cut out; those receive a green Qualified label. See [What are Marvel Value Stamps?](/guides/what-are-marvel-value-stamps).
2. **Ordinary 1974 handling.** Newsstand copies were read, not bagged.
3. **Restoration.** Because the book is worth restoring, a meaningful share of copies on the market are purple-label. See [What does restored mean?](/guides/what-does-restored-mean-on-a-comic-label).

## What to check before buying

- Label colour: blue for unrestored, green for a missing stamp, purple for restoration.
- Stamp status on the label notes.
- Certification number verified on the grader's site.
- Printing: Marvel has reissued the story many times, including facsimiles.

## In the store

Two copies show the range: an unrestored [CGC 3.5](/store/incredible-hulk-181-cgc-3-5) and a [CBCS 2.0 restored copy](/store/incredible-hulk-181-cbcs-2-0-restored). See also [First appearance of Wolverine](/guides/first-appearance-of-wolverine) and the [Wolverine character page](/characters/wolverine).

faq.q: Is Incredible Hulk #180 worth buying instead?
faq.a: It is the true first appearance, as a one-panel cameo, and costs a fraction of #181. Many collectors own both. The market will always price #181 as the key.

faq.q: How can I tell a reprint of Hulk #181?
faq.a: Check the cover price (25 cents on the original), the indicia date, and the absence of a modern barcode. Facsimiles state that they are facsimiles in the indicia.

title: Why is Amazing Spider-Man #129 a key issue?
answer: Amazing Spider-Man #129 (February 1974) is the first appearance of the Punisher and of the Jackal, the villain behind the original Clone Saga. Gerry Conway wrote it, Ross Andru drew it and John Romita Sr. designed the Punisher's skull costume. It is one of the three headline Bronze Age keys with Incredible Hulk #181 and Giant-Size X-Men #1.
body:
## The story

The Jackal hires the Punisher to kill Spider-Man, framing him for a murder; the Punisher realises he has been used and walks away. The character was meant to be a one-off. Reader response brought him back in #134–135, and by the 1980s he carried his own titles.

## Two keys in one

- **The Punisher** — the reason the book is expensive.
- **The Jackal** — Miles Warren, who returns in #148–149 with the first Spider-Man clone and drives the 1990s Clone Saga.

## Collecting notes

- **Marvel Value Stamp**: the issue contains one; a cut stamp means a qualified label.
- **Grade curve**: 9.8 copies carry a very large premium over 9.4 and 9.6, because high-grade survivors are limited.
- **Reprints**: Marvel Tales, a 1990s reprint, and modern facsimiles exist.

A [CBCS 8.5 copy is in the store](/store/amazing-spider-man-129-cbcs-8-5). See [First appearance of the Punisher](/guides/first-appearance-of-punisher), the [Punisher character page](/characters/punisher) and the [Spider-Man character page](/characters/spider-man).

title: Giant-Size X-Men #1 vs X-Men #94: which is the key?
answer: Both. Giant-Size X-Men #1 (May 1975) introduces the new team — first appearances of Storm, Nightcrawler, Colossus and Thunderbird — and is the more valuable book. X-Men #94 (August 1975) is the first regular issue of the new team, the first issue written by Chris Claremont, and the start of the run that made the X-Men Marvel's best-selling franchise. Collectors treat Giant-Size #1 as the first appearance key and #94 as the first-issue key.
body:
## Giant-Size X-Men #1

A 68-page special by Len Wein and Dave Cockrum that reintroduced the X-Men after five years of reprints. Professor X assembles Storm, Nightcrawler, Colossus, Thunderbird, Wolverine, Banshee and Sunfire to rescue the original team from Krakoa. Four major characters debut here and Wolverine joins the team. The square-bound spine and thick page count make high-grade copies scarce.

## X-Men #94

The first regular issue after the Giant-Size, with Claremont scripting Wein's plot and Cockrum drawing. Most of the original team leaves; Thunderbird dies in #95. Claremont wrote the title continuously until 1991, and #94 is where the sixteen-year run begins.

## How the market treats them

| | Giant-Size X-Men #1 | X-Men #94 |
|---|---|---|
| Cover date | May 1975 | August 1975 |
| Why it is a key | First Storm, Nightcrawler, Colossus, Thunderbird; new team | First regular issue of the new team; Claremont's first issue |
| Relative value | Higher | Lower but still a top Bronze Age key |
| High-grade scarcity | Very scarce (square-bound) | Scarce |
| Marvel Value Stamp | Yes | Yes |

## In the store

X-Men #94 is available in three grades: [CGC 9.2](/store/x-men-94-cgc-9-2), [CGC 9.2 with off-white pages](/store/x-men-94-cgc-9-2-off-white) and [CGC 8.0](/store/x-men-94-cgc-8-0) — a useful comparison of how page quality is priced at the same grade. See [First appearance of Storm](/guides/first-appearance-of-storm), [What is page quality?](/guides/what-is-page-quality) and the [X-Men character page](/characters/x-men).

title: Avengers #4 explained: the return of Captain America
answer: Avengers #4 (March 1964), by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby, revives Captain America, found frozen in ice by the Avengers and made a member. It is his first Silver Age appearance and first appearance in the modern Marvel Universe, which is why it is the most valuable issue of the early Avengers run after #1 and one of the major Silver Age keys.
body:
## The story

The Sub-Mariner throws a block of ice into the sea; the Avengers pull a costumed body from it. Cap wakes, remembers Bucky's death, and joins the team within the issue. Kirby, who co-created the character in 1941, drew the return. The Golden Age Captain America continuity — including the 1950s revival — was later explained away as other men in the costume.

## Why it matters

- First Silver Age Captain America.
- Cap becomes the Avengers' leader, the role he has held for most of the title's history.
- Marvel's first explicit link between its Golden Age and its 1960s line.

## Collecting

High-grade copies are scarce. The Golden Record reprint (1966) and a Marvel Milestone Edition exist. A [CGC 6.5 is in the store](/store/avengers-4-cgc-6-5), and the store also has Avengers #1, #48, #57, #87 and #100 — see [First appearance of the Avengers](/guides/first-appearance-of-avengers) for the list. See also [First appearance of Captain America](/guides/first-appearance-of-captain-america) and the [Captain America character page](/characters/captain-america).

title: Strange Tales #135: the first appearance of S.H.I.E.L.D. and Hydra
answer: Strange Tales #135 (August 1965), by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby, reintroduced Nick Fury as the modern-day director of S.H.I.E.L.D. and, in the same issue, introduced S.H.I.E.L.D. itself, the Helicarrier, the Life Model Decoy and Hydra. It is a Silver Age key whose importance grew with the organisation's central role in Marvel's films and television.
body:
## The issue

Strange Tales had been split between the Human Torch and Doctor Strange. With #135, the Torch's feature was replaced by "Nick Fury, Agent of S.H.I.E.L.D.", with Fury (from Sgt. Fury and His Howling Commandos) recruited by Tony Stark to lead an international espionage agency against Hydra. Kirby designed the Helicarrier and the gadgets in a single 12-page story.

## Firsts in this issue

- S.H.I.E.L.D. (then Supreme Headquarters, International Espionage, Law-Enforcement Division)
- Hydra
- The Helicarrier
- The Life Model Decoy
- Nick Fury as a present-day character

## Collecting

Strange Tales #135 was a modest key until the films; it is now one of the better-known Silver Age Marvels. A [CGC 7.0 copy is in the store](/store/strange-tales-135-cgc-7-0), alongside [Sgt. Fury #1](/store/sgt-fury-and-his-howling-commandos-1-cgc-4-0), Fury's true first appearance, and [Strange Tales #110](/store/strange-tales-110-cbcs-5-0), the first Doctor Strange. See [First appearance of Nick Fury](/guides/first-appearance-of-nick-fury) and [First appearance of Doctor Strange](/guides/first-appearance-of-doctor-strange).

title: Silver Surfer (1968): a collector's guide to the 18-issue run
answer: Silver Surfer #1–18 (August 1968 – September 1970) is one of the most collected Silver Age runs: every issue is written by Stan Lee, the first seventeen are drawn by John Buscema and the last by Jack Kirby, and the run is short enough to complete. The keys are #1 (origin, 25-cent giant), #3 (first Mephisto) and #4 (Thor cover, the scarcest issue). Early issues are square-bound and chip at the spine, which makes high grades hard.
body:
## The run at a glance

| Issues | Format | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| #1–7 | 25-cent, square-bound, 39-page lead stories with backups | Origin in #1; Mephisto in #3; Thor in #4; Frankenstein's monster in #7 |
| #8–18 | Regular 15-cent format | Mephisto returns #8–9; Spider-Man #14; the Inhumans #18 |

## The keys

- **#1** (August 1968) — origin of Norrin Radd and Zenn-La; a Watcher backup. The most valuable issue in high grade and a Silver Age key in its own right.
- **#3** (December 1968) — first appearance of Mephisto. Second most valuable.
- **#4** (February 1969) — Thor vs the Surfer, with a famous Buscema cover. Widely regarded as the scarcest issue of the run, which is why a 9.0 or better commands a premium out of proportion to its story.
- **#18** (September 1970) — the last issue, drawn by Kirby, with the Surfer's furious "never again" ending.

## Condition notes

The square-bound giants (#1–7) have glued spines that split and chip; look for spine stress, chipping at the spine ends and a loose cover. The 15-cent issues grade more normally. Page quality on this run is often off-white; white pages are a premium.

## In the store

[#1 CGC 6.5](/store/silver-surfer-1-cgc-6-5), [#1 CGC 6.0](/store/silver-surfer-1-cgc-6-0), [#1 CBCS 8.5 with verified signature](/store/silver-surfer-1-cbcs-8-5), [#3 CGC 8.0](/store/silver-surfer-3-cgc-8-0), [#3 CGC 8.5](/store/silver-surfer-3-cgc-8-5), [#4 CGC 8.0](/store/silver-surfer-4-cgc-8-0). See [First appearance of the Silver Surfer](/guides/first-appearance-of-silver-surfer), [First appearance of Mephisto](/guides/first-appearance-of-mephisto) and the [Silver Surfer character page](/characters/silver-surfer).

title: Bronze Age horror: how the 1971 Code change created Tomb of Dracula, Werewolf by Night and Ghost Rider
answer: The Comics Code's 1971 revision allowed vampires, werewolves and ghouls back into comics when handled in the tradition of classic literature. Marvel responded with a horror line that produced some of the Bronze Age's most valuable keys: Werewolf by Night (Marvel Spotlight #2, February 1972), Tomb of Dracula #1 (April 1972), Ghost Rider (Marvel Spotlight #5, August 1972), Blade (Tomb of Dracula #10, July 1973) and Moon Knight (Werewolf by Night #32, August 1975).
body:
## Before 1971

The original 1954 Code banned vampires and werewolves outright and the words "horror" and "terror" from titles. Marvel's monsters of the 1960s were science fiction: giant creatures from space, gamma bombs, scientific vampires such as Morbius. See [What was the Comics Code Authority?](/guides/what-is-the-comics-code-authority).

## The revision

In 1971 the Comics Magazine Association of America rewrote the Code. Among the changes, supernatural creatures were permitted when presented "in the classic tradition" of Frankenstein, Dracula and similar works. Marvel moved within months.

## The keys the revival produced

| Issue | Cover date | First appearance |
|---|---|---|
| Marvel Spotlight #2 | February 1972 | Werewolf by Night (Jack Russell) |
| Tomb of Dracula #1 | April 1972 | Marvel's Dracula series; Neal Adams cover |
| Marvel Spotlight #5 | August 1972 | Ghost Rider (Johnny Blaze) |
| Tomb of Dracula #10 | July 1973 | Blade |
| Werewolf by Night #32 | August 1975 | Moon Knight |

Marvel also launched Monster of Frankenstein, Man-Thing (from Savage Tales #1 and Adventure into Fear) and the black-and-white magazines Dracula Lives and Vampire Tales, which sat outside the Code entirely.

## Why these books are valuable now

Each of the characters above became a film or streaming lead between 1998 and 2022, and each first appearance is a Bronze Age key with a distinctive dark cover that shows wear, so high grades are scarce. Three are in the store: [Marvel Spotlight #5](/store/marvel-spotlight-5-cgc-7-5), [Tomb of Dracula #10](/store/tomb-of-dracula-10-cgc-8-0) and [Werewolf by Night #32](/store/werewolf-by-night-32-cgc-7-5).

See [First appearance of Ghost Rider](/guides/first-appearance-of-ghost-rider), [First appearance of Blade](/guides/first-appearance-of-blade), [First appearance of Moon Knight](/guides/first-appearance-of-moon-knight) and the [Bronze Age collection](/collections/bronze-age).

title: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles #1: printings explained
answer: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles #1 was printed at least five times by Mirage Studios between May 1984 and 1985, and the printings look alike at a glance. Only the first printing, of about 3,000 copies, is the high-value key. Later printings state the printing in the indicia and are collectible in their own right at much lower prices. Read the indicia before you buy, and grade or authenticate a claimed first printing.
body:
## The printings

| Printing | Date | Approximate run | How to identify |
|---|---|---|---|
| First | May 1984 | about 3,000 | No printing statement |
| Second | June 1984 | about 6,000 | "Second printing" stated |
| Third | February 1985 | larger | Stated |
| Fourth | 1985 | larger | Stated |
| Fifth | 1985 | larger | Stated; later Mirage reprints continue the pattern |

Eastman and Laird printed the first run with borrowed money and sold it by mail and through a handful of shops. Demand from the comics press led to reprints within weeks; the second printing was ordered before the first sold out.

## Why the first printing is worth so much

It is the first appearance of a global franchise, it was printed in tiny numbers by two unknowns, and it is the defining key of the 1980s independent boom. Because it is a black-and-white magazine-sized book on newsprint, high grades are scarce; the market values complete copies in any grade.

## Counterfeits

The first printing has been counterfeited. Known counterfeits differ in paper, print quality and cover stock. Any raw copy offered as a first printing should be authenticated; a slab from CGC or CBCS states the printing on the label.

## Later printings as collectibles

The 1984–1985 printings are affordable ways to own the book, and signed copies with a witnessed signature from Eastman or Laird are popular. The copy in the store is a [1985 printing in CGC 9.6 with a witnessed signature](/store/teenage-mutant-ninja-turtles-1-cgc-9-6), listed with its printing stated.

See [First appearance of the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles](/guides/first-appearance-of-teenage-mutant-ninja-turtles), [What is a Signature Series comic?](/guides/what-is-a-signature-series-comic) and the [Mirage Studios publisher page](/publishers/mirage-studios).

title: Batman Adventures #12 explained: Harley Quinn's first comic appearance
answer: The Batman Adventures #12 (September 1993) is Harley Quinn's first appearance in comics, a year after her television debut in Batman: The Animated Series. It is the most valuable comic of the 1990s after New Mutants #98 and a standard Modern Age key. Because it was printed in large numbers, the value sits almost entirely in 9.8 copies, newsstand copies and the scarcer second printing.
body:
## The issue

"Batgirl: Day One" by Kelley Puckett, Mike Parobeck and Rick Burchett: Harley and Poison Ivy against a rookie Batgirl, in the animated series' art style. Harley wears the red-and-black harlequin costume from the show.

## Editions

- **First printing, direct edition** — the common copy.
- **First printing, newsstand** — same printing, UPC barcode, scarcer in high grade. See [Newsstand vs direct edition](/guides/newsstand-vs-direct-edition).
- **Second printing** (1993) — scarcer than the first; identified in the indicia.
- **Reprints and facsimiles** from 2015 onward — clearly marked and not valuable.

## Where the value is

Most surviving copies were bought by collectors and bagged, so 9.4 and 9.6 copies are plentiful. The premium is at 9.8 — see [Why is a 9.8 worth so much more?](/guides/why-is-a-9-8-worth-so-much-more) — and for newsstand and second-printing copies in high grade. A [CGC 9.8 is in the store](/store/batman-adventures-12-cgc-9-8).

See [First appearance of Harley Quinn](/guides/first-appearance-of-harley-quinn), the [Harley Quinn character page](/characters/harley-quinn) and the [Modern Age collection](/collections/modern-age).

title: Amazing Spider-Man #8: the Living Brain and the Human Torch backup
answer: Amazing Spider-Man #8 (January 1964), by Stan Lee and Steve Ditko, is the first appearance of the Living Brain and the issue in which Peter Parker finally fights Flash Thompson in a boxing match. It also carries a six-page Human Torch backup drawn by Jack Kirby — his only Spider-Man story in the early run — which makes it a minor key with unusual appeal to both Ditko and Kirby collectors.
body:
## The issue

The lead story brings the Living Brain, a computer that deduces Spider-Man's identity, to Midtown High, and stages the long-awaited Parker–Thompson fight. The backup, "Spider-Man Tackles the Torch!", has Kirby pencils with Ditko inks — the only time the two drew Spider-Man together.

## Collecting

Early Amazing Spider-Man issues below #15 are all collectible, with #1–4 and #14 as the major keys. #8 is a sensible entry point into the Ditko run: a Kirby-Ditko collaboration, a first appearance, and a grade curve less steep than the villain debuts. A [CGC 8.0 is in the store](/store/amazing-spider-man-8-cgc-8-0).

See [First appearance of Spider-Man](/guides/first-appearance-of-spider-man) and the [Spider-Man character page](/characters/spider-man).

title: Marvel Team-Up #141 and Amazing Spider-Man #252: the first black costume
answer: Spider-Man's black costume — later the symbiote and Venom — first appeared in regular continuity in two issues with the same May 1984 cover date, released the same week: Amazing Spider-Man #252 and Marvel Team-Up #141. Amazing Spider-Man #252 is the more famous and valuable, but Marvel Team-Up #141 is the same in-continuity debut and trades at a fraction of the price. The costume's origin was told in Secret Wars #8 (December 1984).
body:
## The sequence

Marvel's Secret Wars limited series (1984–1985) sent the heroes to Battleworld; the regular titles jumped ahead and showed them returning. Spider-Man came back in a black costume in Amazing Spider-Man #252, Marvel Team-Up #141 and Peter Parker, the Spectacular Spider-Man #90, all cover-dated May 1984. The explanation — an alien costume from a machine on Battleworld — arrived seven months later in Secret Wars #8.

## Which is the key?

- **Amazing Spider-Man #252** is the flagship title and the copy most collectors want; its Ron Frenz cover is iconic.
- **Marvel Team-Up #141** was released the same week and is listed by CGC as a first black costume appearance. It is the value option.
- **Secret Wars #8** is the origin of the costume and the first appearance of the symbiote as a creature.

## Collecting

All three are 1984 direct-market books that survive in high grade; the market is a 9.8 market with a newsstand premium. A [Marvel Team-Up #141 in CGC 9.8 is in the store](/store/marvel-team-up-141-cgc-9-8). See the [Spider-Man character page](/characters/spider-man).

title: Collecting EC Comics: Shock SuspenStories, Panic and the pre-Code line
answer: EC Comics, published by William Gaines from 1947 to 1956, produced the most acclaimed horror, crime, science-fiction and satire comics of the Golden Age: Tales from the Crypt, The Vault of Horror, The Haunt of Fear, Shock SuspenStories, Crime SuspenStories, Weird Science, Weird Fantasy, Mad and Panic. The line was destroyed by the 1954 Comics Code; only Mad survived. EC books are collected for their art, and Gaines File copies set the high-grade benchmark.
body:
## The titles

| Title | Years | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Tales from the Crypt, Vault of Horror, Haunt of Fear | 1950–1955 | The horror trio, hosted by the Crypt-Keeper, Vault-Keeper and Old Witch |
| Shock SuspenStories | 1952–1955 | Social-issue and crime shockers; #1 is cover-dated February–March 1952 |
| Crime SuspenStories | 1950–1955 | Crime; #22's axe cover was shown at the 1954 Senate hearing |
| Weird Science, Weird Fantasy | 1950–1953 | Science fiction, with Wally Wood and Al Williamson |
| Mad | 1952– | Harvey Kurtzman's satire; became a magazine in 1955 and outlived the Code |
| Panic | 1954–1956 | Mad's sister title, edited by Al Feldstein; #1 was banned in Massachusetts for its Christmas parody |

## The artists

EC's reputation rests on its artists: Graham Ingels, Jack Davis, Johnny Craig, Wally Wood, Al Williamson, Frank Frazetta, Harvey Kurtzman, Bernard Krigstein, Reed Crandall and others. Collectors often buy by artist and story rather than by key issue.

## The end

The 1954 Senate hearings, at which Gaines defended the Crime SuspenStories #22 cover, and the Comics Code that followed made the horror line unpublishable. EC cancelled it in 1955 and, after a short "New Direction" line, published only Mad. See [What was the Comics Code Authority?](/guides/what-is-the-comics-code-authority).

## Collecting EC

- **Gaines File copies** — Gaines kept file copies of every issue; they came to market in the 1980s and are the finest known copies of most EC books. See [What is a pedigree comic?](/guides/what-is-a-pedigree-comic).
- Pre-Code horror generally, and the classic covers in particular, carry premiums across publishers.
- Reprints: Russ Cochran's Complete EC Library and Gemstone's 1990s reprints are clearly marked.

In the store: [Shock SuspenStories #1](/store/shock-suspenstories-1-cgc-6-0) and [Panic #5](/store/panic-5-cbcs-9-8). See the [EC Comics publisher page](/publishers/ec-comics) and the [Golden Age collection](/collections/golden-age).

title: New Mutants #98 explained: the Deadpool key and its editions
answer: New Mutants #98 (February 1991) is the first appearance of Deadpool, Gideon and Domino (Copycat), by Fabian Nicieza and Rob Liefeld, two issues before the title became X-Force. It is the most valuable comic of the 1990s. Supply is large, so the market is concentrated at 9.8; newsstand copies, which are much scarcer, and the second printing carry premiums, and several reprints and facsimiles exist.
body:
## Editions and what they are worth

| Edition | How to identify | Market |
|---|---|---|
| First printing, direct | Liefeld cover, no UPC | The standard copy; 9.8 premium |
| First printing, newsstand | UPC barcode on cover | Scarcer; premium in high grade |
| Second printing | Stated in indicia | Scarcer than first; premium |
| Gold and silver ink reprints | Promotional editions from the 1990s | Separate collectibles |
| Facsimiles and later reprints | Stated; modern price and barcode | Low value |

## Why it matters

Deadpool went from a villain in a Liefeld issue to one of Marvel's most published characters and a film franchise from 2016. Every appearance since is downstream of this issue. See [First appearance of Deadpool](/guides/first-appearance-of-deadpool).

## Buying notes

- Check the edition on the scan (barcode area and indicia).
- A 9.6 is a good-looking copy at a fraction of the 9.8 price; see [Why is a 9.8 worth so much more?](/guides/why-is-a-9-8-worth-so-much-more).
- A [CGC 9.6 is in the store](/store/new-mutants-98-cgc-9-6).

See the [Deadpool character page](/characters/deadpool) and the [Copper Age collection](/collections/copper-age).

title: Superman #2 (1939): the second issue of the first superhero title
answer: Superman #2, cover-dated Fall 1939, is the second issue of the first comic devoted to a single superhero, with Joe Shuster's cover of Superman lifting a car. Like Superman #1 it reprinted and expanded early Action Comics stories alongside new material. It is a Golden Age key in its own right — far more affordable than #1, but scarce in any grade and one of the earliest Superman solo issues a collector can realistically own.
body:
## The book

Superman's own title launched in Summer 1939 as a quarterly. Issue #2 continued the pattern of reprinting Siegel and Shuster's Action Comics strips with new pages and a two-page Superman text feature. The early issues sold in enormous numbers by the standards of the time and were read to pieces.

## Collecting early Superman

| Issue | Cover date | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Superman #1 | Summer 1939 | First solo title; a CGC 7.0 sold privately for 5.3 million dollars in 2022 |
| Superman #2 | Fall 1939 | Second issue; car-lifting cover |
| Superman #3 | Winter 1940 | Third issue |
| Superman #4 | Spring 1940 | Second Luthor appearance |

All early issues survive mostly in low and mid grade; restoration is common and a blue label is worth paying for. A [CBCS 3.0 copy of #2 is in the store](/store/superman-2-cbcs-3-0).

See [First appearance of Superman](/guides/first-appearance-of-superman), the [Superman character page](/characters/superman) and the [Golden Age collection](/collections/golden-age).

title: Sub-Mariner #1 (1968): Namor's Silver Age solo series
answer: Sub-Mariner #1 (May 1968), by Roy Thomas and John Buscema, launched Namor's first solo title of the Silver Age after his feature in Tales to Astonish ended. It is one of the 1968 Marvel expansion #1s — with Captain America #100, Iron Man #1, Silver Surfer #1 and Nick Fury #1 — and a solid Silver Age key with a Buscema origin retelling. Namor himself dates from Marvel Comics #1 (1939) by Bill Everett.
body:
## Background

Namor, created by Bill Everett for Marvel Comics #1 (October 1939), was Timely's first major character alongside the Human Torch. Revived in Fantastic Four #4 (May 1962), he shared Tales to Astonish with the Hulk from #70 to #101, then had a single issue of Iron Man and Sub-Mariner (April 1968) before his own title.

## The issue

Thomas and Buscema retold Namor's origin in the first issue and set up the run that followed. Buscema drew the early issues; the series ran 72 issues to 1974.

## Collecting

The 1968 #1s are a natural set for Silver Age collectors, and Sub-Mariner #1 is among the more affordable of them. A [CGC 8.0 is in the store](/store/sub-mariner-1-cgc-8-0). Namor's Golden Age appearances — Marvel Comics #1 and Marvel Mystery Comics — are in a different price class; a [Marvel Mystery Comics #19 (May 1941) is in the store](/store/marvel-mystery-comics-19-cbcs-7-0).

See the [Silver Age collection](/collections/silver-age) and the [Timely Comics publisher page](/publishers/timely-comics).
